summary: Describes a graphics loader on the Project MAC PDP-10 that lets remote ARPANET users send display programs to the Evans and Sutherland LDS-1 and run them repeatedly. Local users can also use it for ARDS and Imlac consoles.

eli5.summary: A way to mail a drawing program to a faraway picture machine, which can then show it again and again.

how could remote users use the lds-1 display

subtitle: Remote access to the Evans and Sutherland graphics display via ARPANET.

tldr.problem: Users on the ARPANET wanted to use the high-end Evans and Sutherland Line Drawing System (LDS-1) display at Project MAC for graphics work, but they were at different locations on the network.
tldr.mechanism: The Graphics Loader lets remote users send a display program once, then execute it repeatedly from the network with different data, while receiving only the generated graphics output back.
tldr.outcome: Remote ARPANET users could develop and refine graphics programs without visiting Project MAC, reducing program transmission overhead and enabling efficient remote visualization.

today: This RFC describes an early remote graphics service on the ARPANET. It represents the challenges of sharing specialized hardware across a network and the techniques used to minimize data transmission while supporting interactive graphics development.

sections.title: Remote Graphics Rendering
sections.content:
The Evans and Sutherland Line Drawing System Model 1 (LDS-1) at Project MAC's Dynamic Modeling and Computer Graphics group is a high-end graphics display device. Users on the ARPANET wanted access to it for generating graphics output from programs they wrote, but sending large programs repeatedly over the network would be inefficient.

The Graphics Loader solves this by letting a remote user send the bulk of a display program once, then send only changes or new data to re-execute it. The output that would normally be displayed at the LDS-1 is instead transmitted to the originating site in digital form.
sections.eli5: A fancy picture machine is at MIT. Instead of sending the whole drawing program each time you want a new picture, you send it once and then just send the numbers that changed.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
Display programs are loaded into memory on the Project MAC PDP-10 and executed when requested. The Evans and Sutherland display has a Writer Address Register (WAR) that captures the coordinates of visible line segments drawn during execution. The Graphics Loader sets up this register before each execution, runs the program, and captures the output coordinates.

Programs must follow strict conventions: they are assembled absolutely, start at memory location 1000 octal (512 decimal), and jump to location 777 octal (511 decimal) when one frame is complete. The Graphics Loader initializes the WAR before execution and saves its final value to determine how much output was generated.
sections.eli5: The display machine runs the drawing program when you ask it to, and it writes down all the lines it draws. Then it sends those line coordinates back to you.

sections.title: The Six Operations
sections.content:
Remote users communicate with the Graphics Loader using six types of requests, each identified by an operation number in a 36-bit word: SETUP (1) loads a new display program and allocates space for output coordinates. EXECUTE (2) runs the program and captures its graphical output. TRANSMIT (3) retrieves display program or output data, optionally converting it to ARDS format (ASCII-encoded graphics). UPDATE (4) modifies part of the program and can execute it immediately. FLUSH (5) terminates the connection. MODESET (6) controls feedback (suppress or send acknowledgement messages) and can enable automatic transmission of output after each execution.

Each request can optionally include an argument word with additional parameters. The Graphics Loader validates arguments, sends error messages if needed, and acknowledges successful requests.
sections.eli5: You send commands like 'here is a new drawing program', 'run it', 'send me the output', 'fix this part', or 'stop'. Each command can have extra information.

references.text: Michener, J., "A Network Graphics Loader", RFC 186, July 1971.
